about: Prepared answers, dev split, judged by gpt-5.4-mini (foundry, batch): written by MLflow run 9d60ece7f7a04d60bb826820ed75ede6 in experiment 'daily-drill'. Endpoint and resource names are left out on purpose.

params.split_rule: lessons dealt 60/20/20 within each phase, frozen in prepared_splits.json

answers.notes: It says A won 12 and B won 8 but then later uses the correct 12-to-8 gap; the main risk is that the phrasing 'wrong side' is a bit misleading, though not strictly incorrect.
It is mostly right, but the made-up example about the workspace and catalogs is too jargon-heavy and over-specific for a plain beginner answer, so it misses the lesson’s simple explanation style.
It adds unsupported claims, especially about Azure virtual machines, Azure Cost Management, and splitting shared spend by identity, which are not in the lesson.

It incorrectly says bills jump because something changed in general; the lesson’s point is that a single total hides which feature/model/user caused the jump, so the answer should focus on missing breakdown rather than denying random-looking jumps.
It is mostly fine, but it goes beyond the lesson by treating module outputs/unknown values and real exceptions as established guidance from the lesson.
It includes a made-up detail not supported by the lesson: saying a near miss counts as forgotten, which goes beyond the lesson’s exact-match/checking description.
It’s mostly right, but ‘new column like channel shows up downstream when nobody decided to allow it’ is misleading because the lesson says new columns are allowed by default in this exercise.
It says the burn rate is actual errors over allowed errors, but the lesson defines it as actual failure rate divided by allowed failure rate, which should be stated more precisely.
It wrongly says a re-run makes the same ids because they come from the inputs, but it overstates MERGE behavior beyond what the lesson explicitly says.

It incorrectly says 25 questions gives about 20 points margin in the example, but the lesson says 25 questions and 70% could be roughly 50% to 90%, which is about 20 points only as a full range, not the margin phrased that way.
It wrongly says the index stores embeddings for each chunk, but the lesson only says chunks are stored in a search index; it also adds an unsupported claim about the embedding model's input limit.
The third example goes beyond the lesson by introducing a cluster-policy loop and a permissions resource, which the lesson does not mention.
It claims ai_mask reads the whole sentence and uses NER, which is not stated in the lesson and may be misleading.
It says the average is right, but the lesson’s correct answer is that the average is not the best answer because gather waits for the slowest worker, not the average time.
It is mostly right, but saying a replacement is blocked only if the rule catches a plain delete is incomplete because the lesson says replacements include delete and should be caught.
It gives away the lesson’s check logic by explicitly listing the three permission questions and which levels count, which is too close to the exercise answer.
It is mostly right, but it is a bit too absolute in saying the role is unrelated to the question; the key issue is that path coverage is separate from permissions.
It is too permissive: saying the answer is “mostly solid and worth sending” is misleading because the gate would not release all 4 claims when one is unsupported.

It has a factual mismatch: saying a field is SUPPORTED and then suggesting the plan proves it reaches the provider is not part of the lesson’s warning-sign answer, and the DEV/UAT/PROD default example is too loose.

It is mostly right, but it overstates that the system tables are not wrong and says the usage counts are accurate without acknowledging that the lesson frames list-price spend as only a guide, not the invoice.
It is mostly right, but it gives the specific 30-day dollar calculation, which goes beyond the requested explanation of why the naive answer is wrong and why the better answer is better.
It is slightly misleading to say the total always rises a lot because the lesson only guarantees output is more expensive than input, not that the total cost must rise by a lot in every case.
The answer is accurate and explanatory, though slightly more detailed than needed.

It wrongly says the threshold should be tuned on validation and then checked once on test, which is fine, but it also adds precision/recall guidance and MLflow details that are not clearly wrong; the main issue is that it claims a big validation-test gap is a red flag without tying it to threshold m
It says 12 comes from adding the values, but the lesson’s point is that 12 is the mistaken add-up while 60 is the full-grid answer.
It is mostly right, but the example is inaccurate because it says the workspace for DEV could be one stack and the things inside it another, which is not the lesson’s stated split.
It wrongly implies a monthly copy protects data and talks about restoring deleted tables, which is off-target for the lesson and distracts from the real issue: ownership and control.

It says the app answer being passed to the drafter would make the expected facts echo the app, but the lesson says the drafter may see the articles from the trace and never the app’s own answer, so that warning sign is wrong.

It says to use a fixed copy of the whole dataset or a sandbox, but the lesson’s main rule is to record and replay or mark missing calls, not to switch to a live fixed dataset or sandbox as the direct fix.
It says all mistakes show up as failed connections, but the lesson also says wrong-tool matching and out-of-order URLs can produce wrong results, not just connection failures.

It wrongly says prod can quietly fall back to dev_sales; the lesson says prod sets its own catalog, and if a variable is missing the error is reported rather than silently using the default for that target.
It adds an unsupported edge case about trailing slashes and Pydantic normalisation, which is not in the lesson.
It adds several unsupported ideas from outside the lesson, like Terraform moved blocks, Azure portal deletes, resource locks, labels, and approver overrides.
The third point goes beyond the lesson by introducing a multi-agent setup as a different case, which is not stated as a stop condition in the lesson.
It gives away the exercise outcome by saying round 2 should go to ask/ask_human.
It says MLflow swaps double braces to single braces in the saved prompt output, which is not what the lesson states; the lesson only says `to_single_brace_format()` converts for LangChain.

It incorrectly implies that searching for team traces returning nothing or empty token_usage is itself a warning sign, but the lesson only says the tag can be lost outside the traced function and the gateway table is a second source to check.
It introduces an unsupported claim about rerunning causing duplicates/side effects, and it doesn't directly answer the specific comparison of why checking the table is better than rerunning the code.

It introduces inaccurate and off-lesson examples (Azure portal/CLI, terraform destroy, resource groups) and violates the lesson’s world; it is also a bit too jargon-heavy and long for a plain beginner answer.
It explains the mechanism, but it does not directly answer why 'It runs on yesterday's data' is not the best answer or clearly contrast what it gets right versus what it misses in the check question.

The second example is a bit too specific and likely outside the lesson’s stated scope, but the main issue is that it treats provider-specific message shapes as covered by the lesson when they are not.
It adds a new claim about sending emails that is not in the lesson, so it is not strictly supported by the source.

It wrongly says the option is backwards, but the learner asked why 'from lake["gold"] to lake[2]' is not the best answer; the explanation should focus on why that direction is wrong and then contrast it with the correct direction.
It contradicts the lesson by saying you can tell whether quality went up at all, when the point is that with two changes you cannot tell which change caused the improvement.

It incorrectly says scattered data is not one of the three gates, but the lesson says if there are no past examples with right answers you cannot test it, and data not joined up can also mean the idea is not doable yet.

It wrongly says MERGE operates on incoming rows by matching ids and then adds unmatched rows in a general way, but it does not clearly tie back to the lesson’s specific check question that the correct result is three rows, making the first line misleading as the chosen answer is actually wrong.
Saying a friendlier rubric gets 'nothing right' is too absolute; it can reduce false alarms, but it still misses the key issue that it cannot verify the refund record.

It correctly says the gate checks support, not relevance, but it wrongly suggests retrieval or the model are the likely fault instead of focusing on the lesson’s point that the answer can be fully supported and still off-topic.
It introduces situations that are not in the lesson, especially the sandbox/traces advice, which goes beyond the provided text.

It introduces hashing and traffic-skew concerns that are not in the lesson, and it does not answer the asked ‘when does this stop working?’ with the lesson’s intended situations like very small data, changing data, LLM/RAG apps, or larger systems.
It says the record can end up missing a resource or half-written, but the lesson only says concurrent writes could corrupt state and does not support those specific extra details.
It says to pair recall with precision@k and to divide by the smaller of k or the number relevant, which goes beyond the lesson and is not supported here.
It invents specific numbers and a worked comparison that are not in the lesson and also uses unnecessary jargon/math for beginners.

It wrongly says recall@5 is not the right answer because it can’t see order and treats all relevant documents as equally good, but the lesson’s specific question is about lacking relevance grades, so the key issue is that recall still needs relevance labels and does not provide graded relevance.
The first point overreaches by saying changing the percentages breaks the lesson, but the lesson allows choosing a split rule and only warns that the recipe must stay fixed once chosen.

It says staff might warn about tricky cases, but the lesson only supports that staff are a guess and that a hand-labelled test gives the measured success rate; the extra claims are not grounded in the lesson.
The claim that a conversation can cross days is not supported by the lesson and may mislead beginners, even though the core point about using conversation id is correct.

It adds an extra detail not in the lesson by naming specific deploy-time behavior and examples, but the main issue is that it misses the lesson’s phrasing that development mode prefixes names with the user’s name rather than just saying deploys are queued.

It wrongly calls TNR zero because the judge failed none of the bad answers; in the lesson it should be 0/2 = 0%, but it also says the judge passed all 10 and then says it agrees with humans on 8 of 10, which is incomplete/misleading without noting failures separately.
It adds unsupported claims about the model remembering nothing between calls and misstates the LangChain snippet by naming graph as the agent and explaining recursion_limit beyond the lesson.

It introduces catalog bindings, row filters, and Terraform authoritativeness, none of which are in the lesson, and it does not answer the requested ‘when does this stop working?’ examples from the lesson’s actual rule.
It incorrectly says the plan would delete all three containers/data; the lesson says only the first is removed and the later items are replaced because their positions shift.
It says Standard endpoints need Change Data Feed, but the lesson says that requirement is only for Delta Sync indexes on Standard endpoints, not for all Standard use.

It says ‘never declines’ means the over-refusal rate is 0%, which is wrong for the lesson because a model that never declines would instead have the dangerous missed-refusal problem on unanswerable questions.
It says the decision record should be written before the evaluation run, which is not in the lesson and is misleading.
It contradicts the lesson by claiming output tokens usually cost more per token, and it does not directly answer the specific comparison the question asks for.

It says "terraform init daily does not make them agree" without clearly tying the fix to the lock file as the lesson's specific mechanism until later, but the main issue is that it correctly answers the check question.
It uses the wrong paired-check counts and rule for the lesson, so the explanation and conclusion are not reliable.
The shopping-list example is slightly off because it changes the total from 1 to 2 rather than showing two concurrent writes to the same record, but the lesson’s core idea is otherwise accurate.
It never directly answers the learner’s tap about why that phrasing is not the best answer, and it drifts into explaining the broader exercise instead.
It subtly adds an unsupported claim that if the heading never appears the result is empty; the lesson only says to start at the heading and does not define that edge case.
It says a deny rule could block an existing workspace run with no warning, which is plausible but goes beyond the lesson’s exact wording and risks overexplaining beyond what was taught.
It claims a user typing {context} can let users sneak in content, which goes beyond the lesson and is not supported by it.
It adds an unsupported claim that a contradiction means you can’t fully trust the other claims, which goes beyond the lesson.
It incorrectly brings in 401/403 and fail-fast behavior, which are not in the lesson and go beyond the asked explanation.

It says the URL can identify a Unity Catalog function by name, but the lesson only says older workspace endpoint URLs are fixed paths plus names; it does not support using the URL to infer tool details beyond the endpoint pattern.
It wrongly says the SP must be added by hand in Databricks; the lesson says the issue is that the lookup happens before earlier stages are complete, not that manual Databricks entry is the fix.
It is mostly right, but saying serverless gaps often mean no budget policy is attached is too specific and not stated by the lesson.

It gives a misleading explanation about new questions landing in dev and then drifts into shuffling language that the lesson does not use, instead of directly explaining that old questions can move between splits and pollute holdout.
It goes beyond the lesson by introducing large-tool and evaluation advice, and the MLflow mention is unsupported by the provided material.

It wrongly says the lesson’s example had three planted facts including the goal surviving; the lesson names goal, table, and ticket_id, but the example summary forgets the table and ticket id and does not say the goal ‘roughly survived’.
It adds unsupported detail about Unity Catalog and workspace internals that the lesson does not mention, so it is not strictly correct.

It adds advice about a separate notes file and latest-value handling that is not in the lesson, and the second example is slightly off because the lesson is about planted facts and probes, not rewording answers.
It wrongly says naming style causes real bugs; the lesson says naming style doesn’t change what Python does, though it can confuse teams.

It wrongly says the container references the account's name even though the lesson's example is about a Databricks workspace assignment and the question asks only for a plain explanation of why 'Both at once' is not the best answer.
It mostly fits, but saying a rerun succeeds is not a guaranteed warning sign from the lesson and could mislead beginners.
It contains a math error: 5 chunk sizes times 4 values of k times 2 models is 40 runs, not 24 or anything else implied.
The edge case about '(416) 555-0199' is wrong because the lesson’s rule only checks whether a word is exactly 10 digits after removing dashes, so spaces would split it before any phone match.

It says buckets 10 to 49 join the new group, which is correct, but it misreads the check question: the better answer is that nobody is reassigned because the same users stay in the same buckets, so the comparison should focus on who keeps the version when the rollout changes.
The example claim that raw agreement would be 96% is wrong for this lesson’s example, because the lesson says the judges agree 98 out of 100.
The second point is too broad: the lesson only explains two verdicts and does not support recommending a general AC1 for multiple grades.
It slightly overstates that the month-to-month comparison depends on the margin being wrong, instead of first checking whether the answers are clustered by product as the lesson says.
